purpose: Buspirone is used to treat anxiety disorders and to relieve the symptoms of anxiety, such as feelings of tension, worry, fear, and irritability. It can also help with physical symptoms of anxiety like a racing heart or trouble sleeping. It is most often used for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD).
how_it_works: Buspirone works by affecting certain natural chemicals in your brain, particularly serotonin and dopamine, which play a role in mood and anxiety. Think of it as helping to gently balance these brain chemicals so your nervous system feels calmer. Unlike some other anxiety medications, it does not cause sedation or make you feel 'foggy' or 'high.'
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include dizziness, nausea, headache, and feeling lightheaded — especially when you first start taking it. Some people notice nervousness, excitement, or trouble sleeping in the beginning. These effects usually improve as your body gets used to the medication.
warnings: Buspirone can interact with certain medications, especially antidepressants called MAO inhibitors (like phenelzine or tranylcypromine) — do not take these together, as it can be dangerous. Avoid drinking grapefruit juice, as it can raise the level of buspirone in your blood. Do not drive or operate heavy machinery until you know how this medication affects you. Tell your doctor if you have liver or kidney problems.
typical_dosing: The usual starting dose is 7.5 mg taken twice a day. Your doctor may gradually increase your dose up to 30 mg per day, taken in divided doses (meaning two or three times daily). It is important to take it consistently every day — buspirone is not a 'as-needed' medication, and it can take 2 to 4 weeks before you notice the full benefit.
